title: Introduction — A World of Change
paragraphs: On daily walks from her lodgings in Ban Hai into town, Julia befriends Goy, the thirty-three-year-old owner of a dusty stationery store. Goy tells her, matter-of-factly, about the death of her father — Mae Jaeng's police chief, gone at forty-seven from a heart attack at a family dinner — and about how learning anicca, impermanence, helped her bear it. The book's question is born in that store: is Buddhist doctrine actually lived, or is it just for monks?

The scholarly consensus says the latter. Ajarn Somwang at Chiang Mai University, the famous reformer monks, even the head monk of the little Ban Hai wat all tell Julia that anicca is "high Buddhism" — Abhidhamma material, for scholars in Bangkok. Go ask the monks, the villagers are supposed to say. Instead, the villagers keep answering.

The Introduction sketches the valley: about two thousand people, a covered market by the river bridge where Mae Daeng keeps her vegetable stall, two shopping streets, farming hamlets, a Karen Christian village in the western hills, and wats in every neighborhood — each one a social center as much as a sacred one.

At the general goods store near the central intersection Julia meets the family the book will follow hardest: Gaew at the counter, her parents Mae San and Paw Nui, her husband Pan upstairs, quiet charismatic Sen who minds the shop and drinks at night, and eleven-year-old Noi, whose school textbook — read aloud at the counter — lays out the Three Characteristics: anicca, dukkha, anatta. Impermanence, unsatisfactoriness, non-self.

Two deaths bracket the section. Goy's aunt P'Dao drives them into the hills for the cremation of Phra Ao Wat, the old head monk, where the Pali chant sounds over the coffin: impermanent, alas, are all conditioned things. And Uncle Anurak, Gaew and Sen's karaoke-shop uncle, dies drunk in a 4 a.m. motorcycle crash — a funeral whose calm unsettles Julia more than grief would have. Gaew, unbothered by doctrine, is nonetheless afraid of his ghost.

The section closes with ordinations: Noi and ninety-nine other boys take novice robes for the school holidays while their families look on, and the impermanence verses are chanted over shaved heads. Staying the night at the shop-house, Julia hears Gaew reading the same chants to herself before sleep — the first quiet evidence that the "high" teaching lives in low places.
A note on names: everyone in Mae Jaeng, and the town itself, is a pseudonym — but the quotes, places, and facts, the author tells us, are true to life.
